author: Paige Riley
title: Jacksonville tenants struggle after Willow Bend complex shutdown - NewsBreak
text:
By Paige Riley ,
5 hours ago
JACKSONVILLE, Ark. — Families in Jacksonville are scrambling to find new housing after the Willow Bend apartment complex shut down, ending months of unsafe living conditions that tenants say included black mold, raw sewage leaking into apartments, and persistent bug infestations.
Residents say the conditions were so severe, they often felt unsafe in their own homes. “The roaches are unreal. We had raccoons in our attic for a long time. We thought people were living up there,” Darrell Huddleston, a five-year resident, said.
Former owners of Big Country Chateau to pay Arkansas $11.2 million Another tenant said, “No one wants to come see me because it’s terrible. I can’t have company without feeling embarrassed because they won’t fix anything. There’s mold in there — you smell it when you walk in.”
The housing crisis at Willow Bend has been building for years. In 2024, the Jacksonville Police Department declared the complex a public nuisance after responding to more than 2,084 calls between 2022 and 2024, including reports of fights, stolen vehicles, and shootings. The owner was given a 90-day notice to address the issues, but tenants say little changed. “I don’t feel safe at all, to the point where I don’t even like being here,” one resident said.
On Sept. 18, during the city’s most recent council meeting, officials passed ordinance1797 condemning the complex and formalizing the process for relocation vouchers. The vouchers give tenants 60 days to move, with moving and living expenses covered. However, residents say the process has been confusing, with many only learning about their options through social media or news reports.
“For me, I wasn’t ready, I wasn’t looking, so it’s going to take me some time, but hopefully not that long,” one tenant said.
“They’re allowing people who’ve been kicked out to come up there now. I can’t get a hold of anyone right now, but I’m trying,” Huddleston added.
Despite the challenges, tenants say they are looking forward to a safer place to live. “I’m excited. I’m overly excited. It’s just wow — I’ve waited this long to get out of here. I should’ve been gone,” a tenant said.
Huddleston added, “Anything would be better than here. You never know if you’re going to be safe. The place is always doing something — there’s fires. The police are here all the time; I’m sure they’re sick of coming out here.”
